Nestlings of the Amazonian black-throated trogon (Trogon rufus) emerge from eggs incubated at a thermal regime averaging 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with hatching occurring after approximately eighteen days [ab = approximately eighteen days]. At this critical transition, newly hatched chicks weigh only 7.6 grams [Wwb = 7.6 grams], a remarkably low initial mass that underscores the altricial nature of trogon neonates. This modest birth weight, among the smallest recorded for any member of the Trogonidae, necessitates an extended period of intensive biparental care. The altricial nestling stage is characterized by rapid somatic growth, with feathers beginning to emerge from pin sheaths within the first week. Parental provisioning is frequent, with both adults delivering arthropod prey, primarily caterpillars and beetles, to the developing chicks. The nest cavity, typically excavated in decayed tree trunks or arboreal termitaria, provides a stable microclimate that buffers against ambient temperature fluctuations. This developmental phase represents a period of high energetic investment for the adults, as the chicks must more than sextuple their birth mass before they are capable of leaving the nest.

Under conditions approximating the species' active metabolic temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], nestlings achieve fledging at 14.5 days after hatching [tx = 14.5 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling period for a bird of this size. This accelerated developmental schedule likely reflects strong selective pressure from high rates of nest predation in Amazonian forests, where trogon nests face threats from arboreal snakes, primates, and toucans. The downy chicks transition rapidly through feather development, with flight feathers reaching functional length by this time. Fledglings leave the nest cavity but remain dependent on their parents for an additional period of several weeks, during which they learn foraging skills and refine their flight capabilities. The post-fledging dependency phase is critical, as mortality rates among newly independent juveniles are typically elevated compared to those of established territory holders. Juveniles exhibit a duller plumage compared to the iridescent green and yellow feathers of adults, a pattern that may reduce aggression from territorial conspecifics during dispersal.

Sexual maturation in Trogon rufus is reached at 180 days after hatching [tp = 180 days after hatching] when measured at the species' characteristic active temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively late puberty, occurring approximately six months after birth, contrasts with the rapid nestling development and reflects the time required to attain the physiological condition necessary for gonad maturation. Young males begin to develop the characteristic black throat and iridescent green upperparts that distinguish the adult breeding plumage, while females acquire the more cryptic brown and grey coloration typical of the sex. Delayed maturity in this species may be linked to a scarcity of suitable nest cavities, as competition for these limited resources is intense among cavity-nesting birds in neotropical forests. The first reproductive attempt typically occurs the following breeding season, as individuals require time to establish territories and form pair bonds. This extended period of sexual immaturity allows subadult individuals to refine their foraging efficiency and accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of reproduction.

The time since birth at first brood for this species is approximately 547 days [tR = approximately 547 days], measured at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], indicating that individuals do not typically breed until their second calendar year. Females produce a single clutch annually [F_R_i = a single clutch annually], with each clutch containing exactly two eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing exactly two eggs]. This low reproductive output, typical of many tropical forest birds, reflects a life-history strategy characterized by high adult survival and extended parental investment rather than high fecundity. The two-egg clutch is consistent across the Trogonidae family and may represent an evolutionary constraint related to the limited space within the nest cavity and the energetic capacity of the parents to provision offspring. Incubation duties are shared between both parents, with distinct shift patterns observed during the seventeen-day incubation period. The resulting annual reproductive rate, while modest, is compensated by relatively high adult survival rates and the potential for multiple breeding attempts over a long reproductive lifespan.

Adult body mass in this species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining an ultimate wet weight of 56 grams [Wwi = 56 grams], notably heavier than males, which reach 51.5 grams [Wwi = 51.5 grams]. This mass difference, representing approximately an eight percent disparity, is among the larger sexual size dimorphisms observed in the Trogonidae. Basal metabolic rate, measured as maximal oxygen consumption at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], is 77.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 77.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns closely with allometric predictions for a bird of this body size. Maximum documented lifespan extends to 10 years [am = 10 years] under field conditions at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], a longevity that is exceptional for a bird of under 60 grams and indicative of low extrinsic mortality rates in undisturbed habitats. This extended lifespan, combined with the low annual reproductive rate and delayed maturity, positions Trogon rufus as a slow-paced, survivor-oriented species adapted to the stable but resource-limited environment of mature Amazonian forests.
